c1.story:
Look around the room you are sitting in. The paint on the wall, the plastic switchboard, the dye in your shirt, the pill in your drawer, the refrigerant humming inside the fridge. Every one of them passed through a chemical reactor somewhere, very likely in Gujarat. Chemicals is the industry nobody sees and everybody buys from.

That ubiquity is also what makes it confusing to invest in. When someone says they own a chemicals stock, they could mean three completely different businesses wearing the same label. One sells a molecule by the tonne at whatever price the world market sets that week. Another sells a molecule for what it does, a gas that cools without wrecking the ozone layer, a pigment that does not fade, and gets paid for the job rather than the weight. The third does not really sell a product at all: it rents out its reactors and its chemists to a Western company that wants its patented molecule made somewhere cheaper and safer than at home.

Here's the thing. These three businesses respond to the same news in opposite ways. A flood of cheap Chinese supply wrecks the first, dents the second and barely touches the third. A Western customer cutting inventory barely matters to the first and can halve the third's growth for a year. So before you look at a single number, you have to know which door a company walks through.

In chemicals, the label on the stock tells you almost nothing. The door tells you almost everything.

Plenty of Indian companies straddle doors. A large name might run a commodity chlor-alkali plant, a specialty fluorochemicals line and a contract manufacturing division under one roof. That is not a problem; it simply means you value the pieces separately in your head, because the market will reprice each piece at a different moment in the cycle.
c1.read:
The three tiles above are the three doors. Read each tile from top to bottom.

  • The name and the line under it tell you how the product is sold: by weight at a world price, by performance in a small club of makers, or under a multi-year contract.
  • The tickers are listed companies that mostly sit behind that door. Click one to open its stock page. A ticker can appear under two doors, which is the straddling point from the story.
  • The bar is the most important part. It shows how much of the profit the company gets to keep, rather than handing it to suppliers or customers. Commodity sits at the low end because the world price decides its margin. Specialty sits in the middle. Contract manufacturing sits at the top, because once a customer has qualified your plant, switching is slow and expensive for them.
  • The last line is the bet you are making when you buy a stock of that type.

A quick test: pick any chemicals name you own and ask which tile it belongs to. If you cannot answer in a sentence, read its latest annual report's segment table before reading anything else on this page.

c2.story:
Think of the industry as a long kitchen with five stations. At one end, raw ingredients come in through the back door: crude oil, natural gas, salt from the pans of the Rann of Kutch, sulphur, fluorspar dug out of the ground, phosphate rock. At the other end, finished dishes go out to customers who never see the kitchen: paint companies, drug makers, farmers, textile mills.

In between, the ingredients get cooked in stages. Refineries and crackers break crude and gas into a handful of building blocks, the chemical equivalent of flour, oil and sugar. Hundreds of intermediate makers turn those blocks into in-between molecules. Then the specialty and active makers turn intermediates into the ingredient that actually does the job, the thing a customer will pay for by name.

So where do India's listed chemicals companies stand? Mostly in the middle two stations. India does not control the first station: it imports much of its methanol, a large chunk of its PVC, most of its fluorspar. The second station belongs largely to Reliance and the state oil companies. The listed mid-sized names live in the middle, cooking intermediates and specialties, and that is exactly where the squeeze happens when either end of the kitchen moves.

And then there is the rival standing at almost every station at once: China. Chinese producers are integrated from crude all the way to the active ingredient, at a scale no Indian company matches. When China decides to export, it is not one competitor showing up at one station. It is the whole kitchen next door opening its doors.
c2.read:
The diagram has two layers. Read the top layer left to right, then the bands underneath.

The five boxes are the stations, from raw ingredient on the left to the final product on the right. Under each station's name you get what happens there and who stands there. Notice how the names change as you move right: importers and state companies on the left, Indian listed specialists in the middle, brands and end users on the right.

The first band row labels who holds each station. The coloured cells marked as Indian listed sit under stations three and four. That is the visual version of the key point: listed Indian chemicals is a middle-of-the-kitchen business, buying from people it cannot control and selling to people who can switch.

The second band row shows where China stands. Count how many stations it covers. Where the China band sits over the same stations as the Indian band, the two compete head on, and that is where Indian prices have a ceiling.

Use it like this: when you read news about any station, trace it along the row. A benzene price rise at station two, or a Chinese fluorspar curb at station one, is a cost shock that lands on the middle stations a month or two later. A paint company cutting volumes at station five is a demand shock travelling the other way.

c3.story:
Here is the slightly uncomfortable truth about chemicals: almost nobody buys a chemical because they want a chemical. They buy it because they are making something else. That makes chemicals demand borrowed demand. It rises and falls with other industries' fortunes, usually a quarter or two later.

Take a crop-protection active made in Gujarat. Whether it sells depends on whether an Indian or Brazilian farmer had cash to spray this season, which depends on the monsoon and crop prices. But it also depends on whether Bayer, Syngenta or Corteva are sitting on a warehouse full of last year's product. In 2023 they were, and they simply stopped ordering for most of a year. The farmers had not stopped farming. The middlemen had stopped stocking.

Or take pigments and resins. They go into paint, and paint goes onto walls, which means housing, repainting cycles and the mood of the middle-class household. A weak paints quarter is a pigment maker's earnings warning, delivered a quarter early.

This is why a good chemicals analyst reads other industries' results calls more carefully than the chemicals companies' own. The customers tell you the future; the chemicals company tells you the past.
c3.read:
Each tile is one customer group. Read every tile in three lines.

  • The name is who is buying.
  • The second line is what they buy from the industry: actives, intermediates, pigments, gases, polymers.
  • The third line is the important one: what moves that customer. This is your list of things to watch outside chemicals.

A useful way to use the grid is to sort the tiles in your head by cycle. Farming and pharma follow their own rhythms, monsoon and drug approvals. Paints, construction and auto follow the domestic economy and interest rates. Electronics, energy and cooling follow global capex and regulation. A chemicals company selling into all of them is diversified. One selling mostly into a single tile is a leveraged bet on that customer's cycle.

Then cross-check with the doors from card one: contract manufacturers tend to sit behind one or two customer tiles, which is why the loss of a single contract hurts so much.

c4.story:
Strip a chemicals company down to its essentials and it is a spread business. It buys feedstock, sells product, and lives in the gap. Everything else on the profit and loss statement is detail by comparison.

That gap behaves very differently behind each door. A commodity maker does not set either price. Its feedstock follows crude and gas; its product follows Chinese export prices. When both move together it is fine. When China floods the market while feedstock stays dear, the gap closes and profits vanish, sometimes within a single quarter. A specialty maker has more control over its selling price, so more of each rupee of sales survives the raw-material bill, but it spends more on people, testing and quality, the price of being a specialist.

Then come the lines that trip up newcomers. Depreciation is big here, because reactors are expensive. Worse, a new plant starts depreciating the day it opens but takes two or three years to fill, so margins fall while the business is actually getting stronger. That is why the market's favourite chemicals stocks often look worst on paper right after a big expansion.

A builder with falling margins is often a better buy than a coaster with fat ones. The depreciation is the future arriving early.

Working capital is the other quiet line. Exporters wait months to be paid, and inventory of a quarter or more is normal. When a customer destocks, it shows up here first, as receivables and inventory swelling before revenue falls.
c4.read:
The two bar charts walk one hundred rupees of sales down to what is left, for the two main business types. Start at the left of each chart and move right.

  • The first bar is the full hundred rupees of sales.
  • The input bar is the raw-material bill, the biggest bite by far. In the commodity chart it takes roughly seven of every ten rupees. In the specialty chart it takes roughly half. That difference alone is most of the story.
  • The opex bar is power, people and freight. Specialty spends more here, because quality, testing and skilled chemists cost money.
  • The depreciation and interest bar is the cost of the plant and the money borrowed to build it.
  • The last bar is what is left before tax. Compare the two charts: specialty keeps noticeably more of each rupee, even after spending more on people.

These are illustrative mid-cycle shapes, not any company's actual accounts. Hover a bar to see the rupee amount.

Below the charts, the list marks which lines matter for this industry. Notice that gross margin, depreciation, capex and working capital all get a clear yes. Power and fuel gets a sometimes, because it is minor for most companies but the entire story in chlor-alkali, where electricity is the biggest cost. Tax gets a no: nothing about it is specific to chemicals.

c5.story:
If you bought Indian chemicals stocks in 2021, you probably felt like a genius. If you held them into 2024, you probably felt like you had been mugged. Same companies, same management, same molecules. What changed was the cycle.

The boom had three engines firing at once. Covid scrambled supply chains, so customers paid anything for reliable delivery. China rationed electricity to its factories in 2021, knocking out some of the world's biggest competitors. Then Russia's invasion of Ukraine sent European gas prices through the roof, making European chemical plants uneconomic overnight. Orders poured into India. Spreads fattened, and the market paid forty to fifty times earnings for specialty names.

Then the hangover. Customers who had over-ordered for fear of shortages found their warehouses full and stopped buying. And all the Chinese capacity built during the boom came online at once, with nowhere to go but export markets, at almost any price. Product prices fell by a third to a half, Indian margins shrank, and many stocks halved.

Today the industry sits in an awkward early up-cycle. Volumes are back, because customer destocking has run its course. Prices are not, because China still has too much capacity. The recovery is coming through the volume line, not the price line, which is the slower, grindier kind.
c5.read:
Three pieces work together here: the clock, the timeline and the four hands.

The clock is a circle split into four arcs: boom, peak, bust and bottom, in that order clockwise, starting at the top. The years under each arc are when the last full cycle went through that phase. The arrow from the centre points to where the industry is today; for chemicals it sits just past the bottom, heading up into the boom arc. Hover an arc to read what defined that phase.

The timeline next to it tells the same story year by year from 2019. The colour of each entry tells you its tone: boom years, bust years, neutral years and the latest entry marked as now. Read it once top to bottom and you have the whole cycle in a minute.

The four hands are what you watch to move the arrow yourself, without waiting for anyone's opinion.

  • Chinese export prices: the ceiling on Indian prices. Flat now. When they rise, the cycle is turning for real.
  • Indian gross margins: expanding now. That is the spread coming back.
  • Inventory days: falling, which says destocking is over.
  • Capex and asset turns: capex is rising while turns are flat, a mixed reading. Both rising is a healthy build. Capex rising while turns fall is how the next bust starts.

The readings are as of the date the explainer was written. The arrows beside each hand tell you which way it last moved.

c6.story:
A chemicals company's results are decided, to a surprising degree, by people who have never heard of it. A planner in Beijing deciding whether to let chemical exporters run at full tilt. A gas trader in Amsterdam pricing next winter. A refiner in Jamnagar setting the benzene price. A monsoon forecaster in Pune.

Two of those dials matter more than all the others put together. The first is Chinese export prices, because they are the ceiling on what any Indian maker can charge. When China is dumping, it does not matter how efficient your plant is; the world price falls to China's level. The second is the European gas price, because Europe is the other big producer. When gas is dear, European plants shut and their customers come to India. When gas is cheap, Europe competes again.

Then there are the two-faced dials. A weaker rupee helps an exporter and hurts a company that imports its intermediates; many Indian chemicals companies do both. A crude oil rise first squeezes the spread, because input costs jump before selling prices catch up, and then passes through a quarter later. And there are the slow, rule-shaped dials: the Kigali phase-down quietly turning refrigerant gases into a licensed business, and EU rules on PFAS that could shut a door on fluorochemical exports.
c6.read:
Each row is one dial. Read across the row in four steps.

  • Dial: the outside force.
  • Channel: the route by which it reaches the industry's profits. This is the most useful column, because it tells you what to look for in the next results call.
  • A rise does: the effect of the dial going up. A green upward arrow means a rise helps the industry, a red downward arrow means it hurts, and a diamond means it cuts both ways depending on the company.
  • Weight: one to three dots for how much it matters. Three dots means it can make or break a year.

The last column shows today's reading where the dial maps to a series we track, like Brent crude or the rupee. Dials without a live series, like Chinese export prices or European gas, show a dash; for those you rely on the news and the companies' own commentary.

The quickest way to use the table is to scan the three-dot rows first. For chemicals those are Chinese prices and European gas, the two the so-what line below tells you to track if you track nothing else.

c7.story:
Every few years someone predicts that India will become the world's chemicals factory, replacing China. It is a good story, and parts of it are coming true. But the bottlenecks explain why it is happening slowly, niche by niche, rather than all at once.

The first is structural and does not go away: China's cost advantage. Chinese producers are bigger, integrated from crude oil to final active, run on cheaper power and are backed by patient state capital. India does not win on cost. It wins on reliability, on intellectual property protection, on being the second source a Western customer wants so it is not entirely dependent on China.

The second is that India imports much of what it needs at the start of the kitchen. When there is a supply shock upstream, Indian makers cannot simply buy locally; the shock lands straight on their spreads.

Then come the surprise risks, the kind worth a news alert. Gujarat's pollution board can shut an entire cluster for weeks. Fires and explosions at chemical plants are a recurring headline, and they bring shutdowns, investigations and sometimes permanent damage to a customer relationship. Getting a new plant approved takes years. And a contract customer typically spends two to three years qualifying a new plant before it places a serious order, which protects incumbents and punishes newcomers.
c7.read:
Each row is one bottleneck, with a plain explanation of why it bites and a severity label. The severity label is the useful part, because it tells you how to think about each risk.

  • Structural means permanent. It caps returns across the whole cycle, so it belongs in your valuation, not your news feed.
  • Recurring means it comes back again and again: pollution closures, plant accidents, seasonal swings in agrochemicals. These are the headlines that move a single stock for a week.
  • Cyclical means it bites in bad times, like funding freezes when rates rise.
  • Two-sided cuts both ways. Long customer qualification slows new entrants, which protects the incumbents you might own.
  • Slow means it is fixing itself gradually, like hazardous-cargo logistics outside Gujarat.

Read the table top to bottom: the first two rows set the ceiling on how good this industry can ever get, and the next two are the surprises that can hit any quarter.

c8.story:
In chemicals, a bureaucrat's signature can be worth more than a new plant. Consider the anti-dumping duty. When the Directorate General of Trade Remedies finds that China is selling a chemical in India below a fair price and the government imposes a duty, every Indian maker of that product gets a price floor for years. Duty extensions have quietly propped up margins for a whole list of products through the downturn.

Then there are the rules that behave like tariffs without being called tariffs. Quality control orders from the standards bureau require imported chemicals to meet Indian standards, which in practice slows imports from the cheapest sources.

Some rules are moats. A pesticide registration is hard and slow to get, so a company holding a basket of them has an asset competitors cannot buy quickly. The Kigali amendment to the Montreal Protocol caps refrigerant gas production over time, which sounds bad until you realise it turns an existing producer's capacity into a scarce licence.

And some rules are threats arriving from outside. Europe is moving against PFAS, the so-called forever chemicals, and its carbon border tax will tax the carbon in imports. For Indian fluorochemical exporters, Brussels may matter more than Delhi in the next few years.
c8.read:
Each row is a regulator or a rule. Read across: who it is, what it does, why an investor should care, and its status.

The status column is how to prioritise.

  • Always: permanent fixtures, like pollution boards and pesticide registration. They do not make news often, but when they do, it is usually a plant closure.
  • Live: actively shaping prices today. Anti-dumping duties and quality control orders are the live rules to follow here; check the duty dockets for products your companies make.
  • New: freshly introduced, like the chemical parks scheme. Slow tailwinds, not quarter movers.
  • Coming: the rules to prepare for. Kigali quotas and EU rules on PFAS and carbon sit here, and they are the biggest external swing factors for fluorochemicals.

Dated regulatory news for this industry, filtered from our feed, sits on the Picks and signals tab.

c9.story:
Michael Porter's five forces is a fancy name for a simple question: once the money comes in, who gets to keep it? Suppliers can squeeze you on input prices. Customers can squeeze you on selling prices. Rivals can start a price war. Newcomers can crowd in. And substitutes can make your product unnecessary.

Run commodity chemicals through that test and it fails almost everywhere. Rivals are the whole world, led by China, so price competition is relentless. Suppliers are few, and China controls key inputs like fluorspar. Customers switch on price, because a tonne of commodity product is a tonne of commodity product. No wonder commodity makers keep so little.

Specialty and contract manufacturing do much better, mainly because of the buyer column. A Western agrochemical giant that has spent two years qualifying your plant, auditing your safety and testing your batches will not switch to save a few cents. That stickiness is the entire investment case for contract manufacturers.

But specialty has one weakness commodity does not: substitutes driven by regulation. When regulators retire a molecule, as refrigerants moved from older gases to newer ones and as PFAS restrictions loom, a specialty product can lose its market by law, regardless of how well it is made.
c9.read:
The radar chart has five spokes, one per force. The further a shape reaches out along a spoke, the more pressure that force puts on the company. So a smaller shape is the better business.

Two shapes are drawn: one for commodity and one for specialty and contract combined. Look at the overall size first: the commodity shape is larger in almost every direction, which is the picture of a business that keeps little of what it earns.

Then look for the one spoke where the shapes cross. On substitutes, specialty reaches further than commodity. That is the regulation risk from the story: a rule change can retire a specialty molecule outright.

The table beside the chart gives the score behind each spoke, from zero for no pressure to three for heavy pressure, and a one-line reason. If you disagree with a reason for a particular company, mentally redraw its shape; that is exactly how a good analyst uses this framework.

c10.story:
A chemicals results call can drown you in detail: product mix, plant commissioning dates, customer audits, freight. Most of it is noise. Eight numbers tell you almost everything, and you can read them in five minutes.

Gross margin comes first, because it is the spread, and the spread is the cycle. Next comes profit per kilogram, which strips out volume and tells you whether pricing power is real. If volumes are rising while profit per kilogram falls, the company is buying growth with a price cut, which is how price wars start.

Then come the build numbers: capacity utilisation on new plants, asset turns on the new capex, and the ratio of capex to depreciation. Together they tell you whether the expansion is filling up and earning its keep, or whether the company built ahead of demand.

Finally, the risk numbers. Inventory and receivable days tell you about destocking before revenue does. Export share and top-customer share tell you how exposed the company is to the rupee and to the loss of a single contract. And return on capital tells you whether the whole machine earns more than it costs to fund across a full cycle.
c10.read:
The table has one row per number. Read across: the number, what it tells you, what good looks like, and today's industry median.

  • What it tells you is the reason to read it. Ask the question in that column of each company you own.
  • What good looks like gives the benchmark. This is the only column on the page that carries figures, and they are rules of thumb for a typical company, not targets.
  • Today's industry median comes from the latest annual filings of the industry's listed companies in our database. It tells you where the typical company sits right now. A median well below the good mark is a sign of where the cycle is.

The trick is to compare three things for any company: its own number, the industry median and the good mark. A company above the median in a bad year is the kind that comes out of the downturn stronger.

c11.story:
The best warnings about chemicals rarely come from chemicals companies. They come from the edges: a trade-remedy docket in Delhi, a pollution board order in Gandhinagar, a gas price in Europe, an inventory comment from a German agrochemical giant, the monsoon map.

Each of those signals speaks with a different lead time. A new anti-dumping duty or a cluster closure hits the same quarter. European gas and customers' destocking commentary show up in margins about a quarter later. Chinese export prices and the monsoon speak two quarters ahead. The trick is to listen to the early voices and act before the results confirm what they already said.

Combine those signals and you get a simple rule. The industry is genuinely in an up-cycle when three things are true together: Chinese prices are rising, Indian gross margins are expanding, and capex is restarting with asset turns holding up. Two out of three is an early recovery. One is a false dawn. Right now two are ticking, and the missing one is the one that matters most: China's prices. That is why the call favours duty-protected and contract names over pure commodity until China turns.
c11.read:
The chart places each outside signal along a line by how far ahead it speaks. The further right a dot sits, the earlier the warning. Dots on the far left move in the same quarter; dots on the far right speak two or three quarters ahead. Hover a dot to read the channel through which it reaches this industry's earnings.

Use the chart as a reading order. Each quarter, check the dots on the right first, because they tell you about the quarter after next. Then confirm with the dots in the middle. The left-hand dots tell you what is already happening.

Below the chart sits the rule with its three signs. A tick means the sign is on, a cross means it is not, and the short note gives today's state. Count the ticks against the rule above them.

Finally, the call box gives the directional view, the points behind it and, most usefully, what would change it. Treat those last items as your alerts: if one of them shows up in the news, the call is due for a rethink.
